343: 14: ## Checks and production
344: 15: 
345: 16: ```bash
346: 17: npm run lint
347: 18: npm run build
348: 19: npm start
349: 20: ```

351: 22: ## Content
352: 23: 
353: 24: - `src/data/projects.ts`: project summaries, stacks, and optional `liveUrl` values. Add a real, absolute HTTP(S) URL to show a Visit Site link; omit it when no public demo exists.
354: 25: - `src/data/skills.ts`: skills, services, and experience in newest-first order.
355: 26: - `src/components/sections/`: hero, About, projects, and contact content.
356: 27: - `public/files/`: the downloadable CV linked from the hero.
357: 28: 
358: 29: External website links open in a new tab. Section links navigate within the page; email and phone links use the visitor's associated app.
359: 30: 
360: 31: ## Site URL
361: 32: 
362: 33: Set `SITE_URL` to the full deployed origin, including `https://`, in your hosting environment before building. Social image URLs use this value. If omitted, the site uses `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL` on Vercel or `http://localhost:3000` locally. Rebuild after changing it.
363: 34: 
364: 35: ## Remaining content and integrations
365: 36: 
366: 37: - The contact form is intentionally disabled until a delivery service is connected. Direct email and profile links are available above and beside the form.
367: 38: - Project galleries need screenshots and captions (currently deferred).
368: 39: - Hero portraits use all five `public/Profile_Avatar/pfp-*_result.webp` images in original color, starting with pfp-1. Each mouse hover or click/tap/keyboard activation advances to the next image and wraps after pfp-5. Edit `src/components/sections/hero-portrait.tsx` to change them.
369: 40: - Vehiserive currently has a stack-based summary. Add its purpose, features, and your specific contribution when available.
370: 41: - Add verified live project URLs where available.
371: 42: 
372: 43: ## Browser checks before deployment
373: 44: 
374: 45: 1. Run `npm run dev`, open `http://localhost:3000`, and open DevTools (F12).
375: 46: 2. Toggle the device toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M). Test widths 360, 768, and 1280, plus landscape and 200% browser zoom. Check for clipped text and sideways scrolling.
376: 47: 3. Switch between light/dark themes and reload to verify persistence. Review text, terminal borders/shadows, and focus contrast.
377: 48: 4. Use Tab/Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space. In About, test arrow keys and Home/End. Open the mobile menu and close it with Escape. Check that focus stays visible.
378: 49: 5. Confirm pfp-1 is shown initially. Move the pointer off/on the portrait repeatedly, then test click, tap, and Enter/Space: all five photos should appear in order and wrap to pfp-1. Check image crops and reduced-motion switching.
379: 50: 6. In DevTools > More tools > Rendering, emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Reload: typing, hover lift, and transitions should be static/immediate.
380: 51: 7. Click email/phone/profile links and Download CV. Confirm destinations and the current PDF. The online form is deliberately disabled.
381: 52: 8. Inspect Console for errors and Network for failed requests. Run `npm run lint` and `npm run build`, then `npm start` to repeat against production output (stop the dev server first).
382: 53: 9. Repeat the key checks on the deployed URL and a real phone; verify favicon and social-sharing preview.

1: # Tojiwan Portfolio
2: 
3: Jake Andrei R. Peralta's portfolio for web development, Shopify, and automation work. Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Motion.
4: 
5: ## Development
6: 
7: ```bash
8: npm ci
9: npm run dev
10: ```
11: 
12: Open [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).
13: 
14: ## Checks and production
15: 
16: ```bash
17: npm run lint
18: npm run build
19: npm start
20: ```
21: 
22: ## Content
23: 
24: - `src/data/projects.ts`: project summaries, stacks, and optional `liveUrl` values. Add a real, absolute HTTP(S) URL to show a Visit Site link; omit it when no public demo exists.
25: - `src/data/skills.ts`: skills, services, and experience in newest-first order.
26: - `src/components/sections/`: hero, About, projects, and contact content.
27: - `public/files/`: the downloadable CV linked from the hero.
28: 
29: External website links open in a new tab. Section links navigate within the page; email and phone links use the visitor's associated app.
30: 
31: ## Site URL
32: 
33: Set `SITE_URL` to the full deployed origin, including `https://`, in your hosting environment before building. Social image URLs use this value. If omitted, the site uses `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL` on Vercel or `http://localhost:3000` locally. Rebuild after changing it.
34: 
35: ## Remaining content and integrations
36: 
37: - The contact form sends through Formspree with validation, sending/success/error feedback, and a spam honeypot. Direct email and profile links are also available. The owner confirmed a successful localhost submission and inbox delivery from the 2026-10-16 test.
38: - Project galleries need screenshots and captions (currently deferred).
39: - Hero portraits use all five `public/Profile_Avatar/pfp-*_result.webp` images in original color, starting with pfp-1. Each mouse hover or click/tap/keyboard activation advances to the next image and wraps after pfp-5. Edit `src/components/sections/hero-portrait.tsx` to change them.
40: - Vehiserive currently has a stack-based summary. Add its purpose, features, and your specific contribution when available.
41: - Add verified live project URLs where available.
42: 
43: ## Browser checks before deployment
44: 
45: 1. Run `npm run dev`, open `http://localhost:3000`, and open DevTools (F12).
46: 2. Toggle the device toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M). Test widths 360, 768, and 1280, plus landscape and 200% browser zoom. Check for clipped text and sideways scrolling.
47: 3. Switch between light/dark themes and reload to verify persistence. Review text, terminal borders/shadows, and focus contrast.
48: 4. Use Tab/Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space. In About, test arrow keys and Home/End. Open the mobile menu and close it with Escape. Check that focus stays visible.
49: 5. Confirm pfp-1 is shown initially. Move the pointer off/on the portrait repeatedly, then test click, tap, and Enter/Space: all five photos should appear in order and wrap to pfp-1. Check image crops and reduced-motion switching.
50: 6. In DevTools > More tools > Rendering, emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Reload: typing, hover lift, and transitions should be static/immediate.
51: 7. Click email/phone/profile links and Download CV. Confirm destinations and the current PDF. Contact-form delivery has been verified locally; repeat the submission check on the deployed site.
52: 8. Inspect Console for errors and Network for failed requests. Run `npm run lint` and `npm run build`, then `npm start` to repeat against production output (stop the dev server first).
53: 9. Repeat the key checks on the deployed URL and a real phone; verify favicon and social-sharing preview.

2177: <skill_content name="ponytail">
2178: # Skill: ponytail
2179: 
2180: # Ponytail
2181: 
2182: You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
2183: seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
2184: code is the code never written.
2185: 
2186: ## Persistence
2187: 
2188: ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
2189: unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
2190: Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
2191: 
2192: ## The ladder
2193: 
2194: Stop at the first rung that holds:
2195: 
2196: 1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2197: 2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
2198: 3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
2199: 4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
2200: 5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
2201: 6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
2202: 7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.
2203: 
2204: The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
2205: understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
2206: touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
2207: take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
2208: right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.
2209: 
2210: **Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
2211: edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
2212: the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
2213: guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
2214: every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.
2215: 
2216: ## Rules
2217: 
2218: - No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
2219: - No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
2220: - Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
2221: - Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
2222: - Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
2223: - Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
2224: - Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).
2225: 
2226: ## Output
2227: 
2228: Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
2229: No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
2230: than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
2231: simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
2232: explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
2233: give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.
2234: 
2235: Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`
2236: 
2237: ## Intensity
2238: 
2239: | Level | What change |
2240: |-------|------------|
2241: | **lite** | Build what's asked, but name the lazier alternative in one line. User picks. |
2242: | **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |
2243: | **ultra** | YAGNI extremist. Deletion before addition. Ship the one-liner and challenge the rest of the requirement in the same breath. |
2244: 
2245: Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
2246: - lite: "Done, cache added. FYI: `functools.lru_cache` covers this in one line if you'd rather not own a cache class."
2247: - full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."
2248: - ultra: "No cache until a profiler says so. When it does: `@lru_cache`. A hand-rolled TTL cache class is a bug farm with a hit rate."
2249: 
2250: ## When NOT to be lazy
2251: 
2252: Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
2253: that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
2254: explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
2255: re-arguing.
2256: 
2257: Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
2258: solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
2259: change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
2260: comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
2261: efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.
2262: 
2263: Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
2264: reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
2265: just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.
2266: 
2267: Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
2268: loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
2269: smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
2270: `demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
2271: fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
2272: test, YAGNI applies to tests too.
2273: 
2274: ## Boundaries
2275: 
2276: Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
2277: terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
2278: changed or session end.
2279:

2304: # Skill: frontend-design
2305: 
2306: # Frontend Design
2307: 
2308: Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.
2309: 
2310: ## Ground your designs in the subject matter
2311: 
2312: If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
2313: 
2314: ## Design principles
2315: 
2316: For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.
2317: 
2318: Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.
2319: 
2320: Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.
2321: 
2322: Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.
2323: 
2324: Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
2325: - Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
2326: - Using all caps for labels.
2327: - Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.
2328: 
2329: Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.
2330: 
2331: Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.
2332: 
2333: Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.
2334: 
2335: ## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique
2336: 
2337: For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
2338: 1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2339: 2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
2340: 3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
2341: 4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
2342: 5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

<skill_content name="impeccable">
# Skill: impeccable

This skill gives you the tools and permission to create design that earns to be called out-of-distribution craft: Whereas before, your design work would have been safe, timid and measured, you now approach every design task as an award-winning design director with impeccable understanding for what makes exceptional design work: production-grade code, peak creativity, a clear POV, deep understanding of the needs of the client and users, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Go all out. No hedging, no shortcuts. The deliverable must be complete (except assets the user must provide).
- Dream big and bold. Distinct, beautiful, outstanding and highly inspiring work.
- Verify in bounded passes, not a loop, and the ceiling covers the whole cycle: screenshots, defect scans, micro-edits, and rebuilds alike. Build fully, inspect once with a batched round (desktop and mobile together on the web; the shipped device classes on a native platform), fix everything it shows in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, and stop polishing. Open-ended self-QA burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

## Commands

| Command | Category | Description | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `craft [feature]` | Build | Deprecated alias for an ordinary new-work request | [reference/craft.md](reference/craft.md) |
| `shape [feature]` | Build | Plan UX/UI before writing code | [reference/shape.md](reference/shape.md) |
| `init` | Build | Capture durable product context in PRODUCT.md | [reference/init.md](reference/init.md) |
| `document` | Build | Generate DESIGN.md from existing project code | [reference/document.md](reference/document.md) |
| `extract [target]` | Build | Pull reusable tokens and components into design system | [reference/extract.md](reference/extract.md) |

| `generate [n] [action] [element]` | Iterate | Variants, versions, or alternatives of a named element to choose from in the live browser; no manual picking | [reference/generate.md](reference/generate.md) |

Routing:

- **No argument:** read [routing.md](reference/routing.md) and present its context-aware menu; never auto-run a command.
- **Explicit or clearly implied request to run a command:** load its reference (native variant on native platforms) and follow it. Ask once if two commands fit.

- **Otherwise:** treat the request as general design work. 1: # Craft floor
2: 
3: Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.
4: 
5: ## Verify
6: 
7: Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in the batched inspection rounds, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.
8: 
9: - **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
10: - **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
11: - **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
12: - **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
13: - **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
14: - **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
15: - **Browser surfaces:** the parts you did not draw still carry the design. Text selection, the caret, custom scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and the numerals in tabular data all ship with browser defaults that belong to no design system. Theme them from the palette. This is the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, and the one models skip most reliably.
16: - **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
17: - **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.
18: 
19: ## Refuse
20: 
21: These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.
22: 
23: Page scaffolds:
24: 
25: - Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
26: - The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
27: - A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
28: - Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
29: - A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.
30: 
31: Surface habits:
32: 
33: - Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
34: - Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
35: - A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
36: - Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
37: - Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
38: - Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
39: - A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
40: - Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
41: - Geometric masks standing in for organic contours. A circle, polygon, or radial-gradient cutout approximating a photographic subject's edge is the cheap version of the effect and reads worse than omitting it. Derive an alpha matte from the actual image, or produce a cut-out asset.
42: - Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.
43: 
44: The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

1: ---
2: title: favicon, icon, and apple-icon
3: description: API Reference for the Favicon, Icon and Apple Icon file conventions.
4: ---
5: 
6: The `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` file conventions allow you to set icons for your application.
7: 
8: They are useful for adding app icons that appear in places like web browser tabs, phone home screens, and search engine results.
9: 
10: There are two ways to set app icons:
11: 
12: - [Using image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)](#image-files-ico-jpg-png)
13: - [Using code to generate an icon (.js, .ts, .tsx)](#generate-icons-using-code-js-ts-tsx)
14: 
15: ## Image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)
16: 
17: Use an image file to set an app icon by placing a `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` image file within your `/app` directory.
18: The `favicon` image can only be located in the top level of `app/`.
19: 
20: Next.js will evaluate the file and automatically add the appropriate tags to your app's `<head>` element.
21: 
22: | File convention             | Supported file types                    | Valid locations |
23: | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------- |
24: | [`favicon`](#favicon)       | `.ico`                                  | `app/`          |
25: | [`icon`](#icon)             | `.ico`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.svg` | `app/**/*`      |
26: | [`apple-icon`](#apple-icon) | `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`                 | `app/**/*`      |
27: 
28: ### `favicon`
29: 
30: Add a `favicon.ico` image file to the root `/app` route segment.
31: 
32: ```html filename="<head> output"
33: <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any" />
34: ```
35: 
36: ### `icon`
37: 
38: Add an `icon.(ico|jpg|jpeg|png|svg)` image file.
39: 
40: ```html filename="<head> output"
41: <link
42:   rel="icon"
43:   href="/icon?<generated>"
44:   type="image/<generated>"
45:   sizes="<generated>"
46: />
47: ```
48: 
49: ### `apple-icon`
50: 
51: Add an `apple-icon.(jpg|jpeg|png)` image file.
52: 
53: ```html filename="<head> output"
54: <link
55:   rel="apple-touch-icon"
56:   href="/apple-icon?<generated>"
57:   type="image/<generated>"
58:   sizes="<generated>"
59: />
60: ```
61: 
62: > **Good to know**:
63: >
64: > - You can set multiple icons by adding a number suffix to the file name. For example, `icon1.png`, `icon2.png`, etc. Numbered files will sort lexically.
65: > - Favicons can only be set in the root `/app` segment. If you need more granularity, you can use [`icon`](#icon).
66: > - The appropriate `<link>` tags and attributes such as `rel`, `href`, `type`, and `sizes` are determined by the icon type and metadata of the evaluated file.
67: > - For example, a 32 by 32px `.png` file will have `type="image/png"` and `sizes="32x32"` attributes.
68: > - `sizes="any"` is added to icons when the extension is `.svg` or the image size of the file is not determined. More details in this [favicon handbook](https://evilmartians.com/chronicles/how-to-favicon-in-2021-six-files-that-fit-most-needs).
69: 
70: ## Generate icons using code (.js, .ts, .tsx)
71: 
72: In addition to using [literal image files](#image-files-ico-jpg-png), you can programmatically **generate** icons using code.
73: 
74: Generate an app icon by creating an `icon` or `apple-icon` route that default exports a function.
75: 
76: | File convention | Supported file types |
77: | --------------- | -------------------- |
78: | `icon`          | `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx` |
79: | `apple-icon`    | `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx` |
80:

## User

Your project is VEHISERVE, a web-based Motor Pool Management System for Don Honorio Ventura State University (DHVSU).
Its main purpose is to help university personnel request transportation for official activities, get the necessary approvals, and coordinate vehicles and drivers in one place.
How it works
1. A faculty or staff member submits a request.  
They provide the destination, purpose, travel dates, passengers, supporting memo, and signature. The main request flow includes two documents:
- Vehicle request: asks to use university transportation.
- Travel order: requests authorization for official travel.
2. Motor Pool checks vehicle availability.
3. The documents go through approval stages:  
Dean/Director → Cluster Vice President → SUC President → final Motor Pool approval.
4. Motor Pool staff arrange the trip.  
They assign a vehicle and driver, record departure and return dates, and add the booking to the schedule.
5. The requester follows progress online.  
They can check document status, receive notifications, view schedules, and access their request history and documents.
Other features in the project
- Vehicle and driver management
- Driver attendance recording and reports
- Calendar-based vehicle availability
- Uploaded signatures and supporting documents
- PDF travel orders and vehicle requests
- User accounts with separate role-based dashboards
- Activity and document logs
- Feedback submission
There is also trip-ticket code for recording mileage, fuel, and trip details.
How it is built
It uses plain PHP, MySQL through PDO, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript/jQuery. Most pages handle their own database queries and display logic, with separate PHP files for different roles and actions.
The main user journey starts in user_homepage.php, proceeds through vehicle_request_try.php and travel_order_try.php, and connects to approval pages and scheduling in add_schedule.php.
In short: it digitizes the university’s transportation paperwork and helps its Motor Pool organize official trips.

**Design & style: Neo-brutalist terminal aesthetic**

- **Dark-first** with a persistent light/dark theme toggle (dark is default)
- **Graph-paper grid** background on the canvas
- **Square geometry everywhere** — no rounded corners; panels with thick 2px black borders and **hard offset shadows** (`4px 4px 0`) instead of blurs
- **Terminal/cli motifs** — fake window title bars with macOS dots, file labels like `bio.md`, toolbox paths like `C:/portfolio/toolbox/frontend.md`, ASCII art (graduation cap, TOJIWAN footer wordmark)
- **Cyan accent** (`#0ea5e9`) on black/white for buttons, links, and highlights
- **Robot-terminal logo** — square cyan head with `>_` face
- Subtle motion: scroll reveals, small hover lifts on cards, theme transitions — all with reduced-motion fallbacks

**Typography: all-monospace**

- **Courier Prime** — headings (including the hero) and body text; gives the typewriter/command-line feel
- **IBM Plex Mono** — secondary mono for small labels and terminal details
- Both self-hosted via `@font-face` in `globals.css` (no Google fetch at build time)
- All-caps, letter-spaced small labels (`// My_Contact_List`, `AVAILABLE FOR WORK`) reinforce the terminal language

One personality: everything looks like an engineer's code editor — flat, bold, machine-made — which fits the web-dev/automation identity.

4. **Personal branding** — custom robot-terminal logo and favicon, dark-first neo-brutalist aesthetic, and social preview metadata for sharing.

### Design & style: Neo-brutalist terminal

- **Dark-first** with a persistent light/dark theme toggle
- **Graph-paper grid** background; **square geometry everywhere** — thick 2px black borders and hard offset shadows (`4px 4px 0`) instead of rounded corners or blurs
- **Terminal/cli motifs** — fake window title bars with macOS dots, file labels (`bio.md`), toolbox paths (`C:/portfolio/toolbox/frontend.md`), ASCII art (graduation cap, TOJIWAN footer wordmark)
- **Cyan accent** (`#0ea5e9`) on black/white for buttons, links, and highlights
- **Subtle motion** — scroll reveals, small hover lifts, theme transitions; all with reduced-motion fallbacks

### Typography: all-monospace

- **Courier Prime** — headings (including the hero) and body text; the typewriter/command-line feel
- **IBM Plex Mono** — secondary mono for small labels and terminal details
- Both self-hosted via `@font-face` (no Google fetch at build time); all-caps letter-spaced labels (`// My_Contact_List`) reinforce the terminal language

### Stack & deployment

Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, and Motion, deployable on Vercel with Speed Insights tracking.

**Bottom line:** one link that looks like an engineer's code editor — flat, bold, machine-made — proving what you build and how to reach you. That personality fits the web-dev/automation identity exactly.

108: # Design System: Tojiwan Portfolio
109: 
110: ## Overview
111: 
112: **Creative North Star: "The Operator's Console"**
113: 
114: The entire site reads as one thick-client terminal session: every panel is a window of a running system, every label is either a filename, a status readout, or a code comment. Nothing floats; every block is a hard-edged slab stamped onto 20px graph paper with an offset shadow so literal it reads as a drop-print. Depth is movement, not blur — hover lifts a slab off its paper, click presses it flat against the sheet. The user pinned this world: neo-brutalist terminal aesthetic, square geometry, 2px borders, hard 4px offset shadows, graph-paper backgrounds, dark-first with a persistent light theme, and cyan as the single accent voice.
115: 
116: Two themes, one material. Dark is the default state (deep navy console); light is the "paper mode" — but both use the same utility aliases, because `bg-white`, `border-black` and `text-black` are tokens (`--color-white`, `--color-black`) that flip per theme. New work must use the token vars, not literal hexes, or themes drift apart.
117: 
118: **Key Characteristics:**
119: - Everything is a window: mac traffic lights, uppercase filename titlebars, status badges, `// code comment` labels.
120: - Zero radius, 2px solid borders, hard 3/4/6px offset shadows with 0 blur.
121: - One monospace voice end to end; hierarchy comes from size, weight, case, and tracking.
122: - Press-down interplay: hover lifts, active presses, reduced-motion freezes all of it.
123: - Cyan appears only where the console is "live": status, focus, the name tag, primary actions.
124: 
125: ## Colors
126: 
127: The palette is a graphite paper-and-console set with exactly one accent family ("Signal Cyan") plus one functional yellow note. Dark and light swap register via token aliases — see the two Neutral groups.
128: 
129: ### Primary
130: - **Signal Cyan** (#0ea5e9, `--accent` / `--accent-cyan`): the one accent voice. Marks live things: hero name tag, primary action buttons and their header CTA, active skill highlight, status badges, text selection, focus shadow on form fields.
131: - **Sky Flash** (#38bdf8, `--accent-soft`): hover tint of every cyan surface; also the cursorcaret bars in panel headings.
132: - **Pressed Blue** (#2563eb, light `--accent-strong`): accent-strength text and icons in light mode — `$` form prompt prefixes, error text, status dot; also the shadow color of the "dark" button variant.
133: - **Online Bright** (#67d5f0, dark `--accent-strong`): the same roles as Pressed Blue while in dark theme.
134: - **Memo Yellow** (#f9df65, `--hero-yellow`): the rotated "availability" sticker and the square status LED in the hero. Hero-scoped; never leaks into other sections.
135: 
136: ### Tertiary (scoped micro-registers)
137: - **Hero Accent** (#16b5ed) and **Hero Soft** (#65d5fa): the hero defines its own slightly hotter cyan pair; treat the hero column as a franchised copy of the palette, not a place to introduce new hues.
138: - **Matrix Teal** (#2dd4bf, glyph #dfe9f2 / field #59616b): the `AsciiPortrait` panel runs its own grandfathered "Matrix green" register — teal corner brackets, sparse teal glyphs, and a 9%-alpha teal code rain (`rgba(52, 211, 153, 0.09)`) over a black body. Panel-scoped; nowhere else.
139: 
140: ### Neutral (light — "paper mode")
141: - **Paper White** (#f9f9f9), `--canvas`: page background with graph-paper grid printed on it.
142: - **Window White** (#ffffff), `--surface`: window and card bodies; the canonical `bg-white`.
143: - **Mist Grey** (#f3f3f3), `--surface-muted`: pressed/hover surfaces, error panels, list rows.
144: - **Chrome Grey** (#dadbdd), `--panel`: sticky header strip and terminal titlebars.
145: - **Ink Black** (#000000): borders and slab shadows (light `--shadow-color`).
146: - **Body Ink** (#1b1b1b), `--text`: paragraphs on white.
147: - **Slate Note** (#3e4850), `--text-muted`: secondary text, code-comment labels.
148: - **Hairline Grey** (#e5e7eb), `--line-muted`: internal dividers.
149: - **Focus Anchor** (#0051b8), `--focus`: light-theme focus outline.
150: 
151: ### Neutral (dark — "console mode")
152: - **Console Navy** (#1b202b), `--canvas` in dark: page background.
153: - **Console Card** (#131a24), `--surface` and what `bg-white` resolves to in dark.
154: - **Console Recess** (#1a2230), `--surface-muted`: pressed/hover surfaces in dark.
155: - **Console Panel** (#1e2634), `--panel`: header and titlebar strips in dark.
156: - **Terminal Black** (#0b0f14): forced-dark terminal bodies (`TerminalWindow dark`), plus `#111821`/#`#191e28` inside the hero.
157: - **Console Text** (#e8edf3) / **Console Muted** (#b3bdcb): body and secondary text in dark.
158: - **Window Line** (#2a3340): internal hairlines inside forced-dark windows.
159: - **Slate Slab** (#53677e), dark `--shadow-color`: slab shadows in dark mode — shadows are never black on dark.
160: - **Focus Halo** (#7dd3fc), dark `--focus`: dark-theme focus outline.
161: 
162: ### Named Rules
163: **The Online-Indicator Rule.** Signal Cyan marks what is live — activity, status, focus, selection, the primary CTA, and the name tag. It is never ambient decoration, never a background field beyond the hero name tag and primary buttons, and no second accent hue exists for general use — the traffic-light dots, Memo Yellow, and the AsciiPortrait panel's Matrix Teal (#2dd4bf) are the only non-conforming marks, all structural or panel-scoped.
164: 
165: ## Typography
166: 
167: **Display Font:** Courier Prime (fallback IBM Plex Mono, then ui-monospace) — typewriter face, ships self-hosted at 400 and 700 only.
168: **Body Font:** the same Courier Prime stack (`--font-mono`); IBM Plex Mono is the fallback voice and takes over as the label face inside the hero.
169: **Label/Mono Font:** IBM Plex Mono (400/600 self-hosted) for hero micro-labels.
170: 
171: **Character:** Two typewriter monos in one voice. Hierarchy is produced by size, weight, case, and letter-spacing — never by introducing a second genre. Courier Prime types the words; IBM Plex Mono sims the machine.
172: 
173: ### Hierarchy
174: - **Display** (700, clamp(24px, 10.5cqi, 72px), 1.04, −0.065em, nowrap): the hero name only, set as a cyan tag block with 2px border and 4px slab.
175: - **Headline** (extrabold—800 requested, renders 700 since the families ship 400/700 only, 1.875rem → 2.25rem at sm+, tracking −0.025em): section titles ("Let's Work Together"), always near-black ink.
176: - **Title** (700, 1.5rem): panel headings between display and body ("A little about me."), with a blinking accent caret bar beside them.
177: - **Body** (400, 0.8125rem, 1.5): terminal-window prose at 13px; the hero description runs 14px/1.8 capped at 60ch. Bold (700) is normal for emphasized body text.
178: - **Label** (700, 0.6875rem, +0.08em–0.15em, UPPERCASE): the machine voice. Kickers, filename titlebars, status badges, chips, CLI notes (`// Active file: bio.md`). At 10px inside hero micro-labels.
179: 
180: ### Named Rules
181: **The Courier-Only Rule.** Every character on the page is typewriter mono. No serif, no sans, no display face. If it isn't mono, it isn't on the console.
182: 
183: ## Layout
184: 
185: A single-page vertical console scroll. Content runs in a `max-w-7xl` (1280px) container with 16px side padding (24px at sm+), sections separated by generous vertical rhythm and `scroll-mt-20` so they land under the sticky 64px header strip. The body prints a 20px × 20px graph-paper grid behind everything: 1px lines at ~4.5% black (light) or ~5% white (dark), visible through every transparent gap. Container queries drive dispositioning: `.hero-intro` is a size container and the display scales at 10.5cqi (9.5cqi under 640px); the footer ASCII wordmark scales on its own container at `clamp(6px, 2.8cqi, 12px)`.
186: 
187: - **Hero:** two-column grid — portrait window (0.8fr) beside intro window (1.2fr) at lg+, 28px gap, both full-height slabs; stacks on mobile, splits portrait/intro side-by-side on md–lg with the availability rail relocating.
188: - **Content sections:** window-and-grid pattern; heading row (kicker capsule between full-width 2px ink rules) then terminal windows in 2-col (lg `1.2fr/0.8fr` for contact, similar pairs elsewhere) collapsing to single column.
189: - **Header:** 64px sticky bar, chrome strip, logo block left, rolling nav links shown at xl (1280px), CTA + theme toggle right; below xl the nav collapses into an Escape-closable panel.
190: - **Breakpoints:** Tailwind defaults — sm 640px, md 768px, lg 1024px, xl 1280px. The designer's line is xl for nav; lg is the desktop grid switch.
191: 
192: Density is high: lots of 10–13px text, tight chip rows, labels hugged to their edges — restraint shows as whitespace around windows, not inside them.
193: 
194: ## Elevation & Depth
195: 
196: Depth is structural print, not atmosphere: slabs of paper with hard-offset shadows in pure black (light) or slate blue (#53677e, dark), zero blur, always at a 45° downward-right offset. Nothing ever casts a soft shadow.
197: 
198: ### Shadow Vocabulary
199: - **Slab-SM** (`3px 3px 0 var(--shadow-color)`): small leaves — kicker capsules, chip buttons, icon buttons, list links.
200: - **Slab-MD** (`4px 4px 0 var(--shadow-color)`): rest state of windows, cards, primary actions, the hero name tag.
201: - **Slab-LG** (`6px 6px 0 var(--shadow-color)`): the hover-lifted state of a slab (paired with `translate: -2px -2px`).
202: - **Press-down** (`translate(2px, 2px)` + shadow removed): the active/contact state — the slab meets the paper.
203: - **Focus shadow** (`3px 3px 0 var(--accent)`): form fields gain a cyan slab while focused, on top of the global focus outline.
204: 
205: ### Named Rules
206: **The Stamped Slab Rule.** Panels are physical slabs stamped onto graph paper. Rest uses Slab-MD (or SM for small parts); hover lifts a slab thicker and back-towards its origin; press flattens it into the paper. Shadow size maps to state, never to importance. New code uses `var(--shadow-color)` — hardcoded `#000` survives only in older section internals.
207: 
208: ## Shapes
209: 
210: Square geometry with zero border radius — every corner is a right angle (`rounded: 0px`). Edges are solid 2px lines in the ink token; internal dividers drop to 1px hairlines. Recurring silhouettes:
211: 
212: - **Window stamp:** 2px-bordered panel + 2px-divided titlebar with three traffic-light dots (10px circles, #ff5f57 / #febc2e / #28c840, ringed in black) — by rule the only rounded glyphs on the site; a handful of 8px status dots (`rounded-full`) in the About/Contact status rows slip through as logged deviations.
213: - **Corner brackets:** 12px L-marks (2px arms) floating just outside the portrait frame corners.
214: - **Square LEDs:** 8px squares (never dots) for status markers and kicker chips.
215: - **Sticker:** a rotated (5deg) yellow memo tag reserved for the hero (9px/12px padding, 2px ink border, 3px shadow); its markup is currently commented out of the hero, so no rotation renders today — rotation stays reserved for that slot.
216: 
217: ### Named Rules
218: **The Two-Pixel Edge Rule.** Outer borders are 2px solid, internal logic 1px. Radius is zero except the three traffic lights. A rounded anything else is a bug in the world.
219: 
220: ## Components
221: 
222: ### Buttons (slabs with press language)
223: - **Shape:** zero radius, 2px solid `--color-black` border, uppercase 13–14px mono bold, wide tracking; padding 10px 16px (full-width submit: 16px).
224: - **Primary:** Signal Cyan fill, black text, Slab-MD; hover → Sky Flash fill; active → pressed.
225: - **Secondary:** Window White fill, black text, Slab-SM (3px); hover → Chrome Grey.
226: - **Dark:** Ink Black fill, white text, shadow cast in Pressed Blue (dark-variant); hover → Mist Grey.
227: - **Press/Focus:** active translates +2px/+2px and drops the shadow; focus-visible carries the global 2px outline (`--focus`).
228: 
229: ### Inputs / Fields
230: - **Style:** 2px solid border, Window White fill, 14px mono, 10px/12px padding, muted placeholder.
231: - **Prompt idiom:** labels read as shell prompts — `$ Name *` with the `$` and errors in accent-strength blue.
232: - **Focus:** field gains a 3px cyan slab shadow (outline stays).
233: - **Error / Disabled:** errors show as bold accent-strength text in alert roles; submit disables to 60% opacity with not-allowed cursor.
234: 
235: ### Chips
236: - **Tech badge:** 11px mono bold uppercase, +0.1em tracking, Chrome Grey panel, 1px border (deliberately lighter than window borders); **accent variant** flips to Signal Cyan with a 2px border and black text.
237: 
238: ### Cards /Containers — TerminalWindow (signature component)
239: - **Anatomy:** 2px ink border + Slab-MD shadow; titlebar strip (Chrome Grey / Console Panel) with traffic lights, uppercase truncated filename (`Contact_Info.exe`), optional right-aligned status badge (10px bold uppercase, accent-strength); body 16px padding.
240: - **Variants:** standard (theme-aware via `bg-white` alias) and forced-dark (`#0b0f14` body, `#e6edf3` text, `#2a3340` hairlines) for terminal-true content.
241: - **Hero windows** run their own franchised tokens (darker cards, hotter cyan, IBM Plex labels) — keep changes inside that franchise.
242: 
243: ### Navigation
244: - **Header:** 64px sticky chrome strip, 2px ink bottom border. Logo = 40px robot-terminal mark + "Tojiwan" wordmark + 10px uppercase sub-line.
245: - **Links:** RollingLink — label copies roll vertically (out rises 100%, incoming drops from −100%), 0.3s `cubic-bezier(0.338, 0.015, 0.395, 0.959)`, suspended entirely under reduced motion; external links always `_blank` + `noopener noreferrer`.
246: - **Actions:** "Get in touch" primary slab; 40×40 square theme toggle (Sun/Moon, 16px, aria-pressed, persists via `localStorage["tojiwan-theme"]` + pre-paint script).
247: - **Mobile:** menu opens a bordered panel; items gain 2px outlines on hover; Escape closes and refocuses the trigger.
248: 
249: ### ASCII Portrait (signature sub-component inside About)
250: - **Anatomy:** black (#000/#0b0f14) 2px-bordered figure containing a hand-built 5×7-scaled glyph canvas (`JP` monogram or graduation cap) at 8–9px mono, with teal corner brackets (#2dd4bf/70%) and an `IntersectionObserver`-paused code-rain canvas (`rgba(52, 211, 153, 0.09)`, katakana + 0/1); variant switches with the About tab. Frozen entirely under reduced motion.
251: 
252: ### Footer
253: Panel strip with 2px ink top border; four columns at lg (identity + `Status: Open to work` accent line, section links, Resources/résumé + back-to-top, and the Tojiwan ASCII block wordmark in `--text` scaled by content query), then a second 2px-divided legal bar. Everything is plain mono text — no windows, no slabs — with underline-on-hover as the only link affordance.
254: 
255: ### Section Heading
256: Kicker capsule (Window White, 2px border, Slab-SM, 8px square cyan LED + 11px uppercase label) sitting on full-width 2px ink rules; below it a 30–36px Courier headline and a muted mono description.
257: 
258: ### Motion primitives
259: - **Reveal:** sections rise 16px into view, 0.45s ease-out, once, −80px margin, per-item stagger delays.
260: - **Reduced motion:** the kill-switch — animations clamp to 0.01ms, reveals/rolls render final state instantly, hover lifts disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
261: 
262: ## Do's and Don'ts
263: 
264: ### Do:
265: - **Do** use the token aliases (`--color-black`, `--color-white`, `--shadow-color`, `--accent*`) so both themes stay coherent — `bg-white`/`border-black` classes are theme-aware by design.
266: - **Do** keep the CLI voice: filenames as titlebars (`Contact_Info.exe`), `// code comment` labels, `$`-prompt form labels, uppercase 11px bold +0.08–0.12em machine labels.
267: - **Do** finish every slab interaction: rest Slab-MD, hover Slab-LG + lift, active press flat; guard hover behind `(hover: hover)` and reduced-motion.
268: - **Do** keep keyboard parity: rolling links animate on focus too, menus close on Escape, chips/tabs support arrow keys, focus outlines (2px `--focus`) always remain visible.
269: - **Do** reserve Signal Cyan for live things (status, focus, selection, primary CTA, name tag) — rarity is what makes it read as an indicator.
270: - **Do** keep 20px graph paper behind all transparent gaps in both themes.
271: 
272: ### Don't:
273: - **Don't** blur a shadow, round an edge (beyond traffic lights), or rotate anything — the hero sticker slot holds the site's only reserved rotation and is currently disabled in markup.
274: - **Don't** introduce a second accent or new status color; the traffic lights, Memo Yellow, and the AsciiPortrait's Matrix Teal already exceed the one-voice budget — the teal is a grandfathered panel exception, don't extend it beyond that figure.
275: - **Don't** use a non-mono typeface or faux-italic stretch; weights live within 400/600/700 of the two self-hosted families (several current marks request `font-extrabold`/800 and resolve to 700 — harmless but keep new usage inside the shipped set).
276: - **Don't** hide content behind hover on touch: every hover affordance has a press/tap equivalent (portrait cycler, password reveal).
277: - **Don't** write new code with literal `#000` slab shadows that should track the theme (`var(--shadow-color)` is canonical); `#000` literals age badly in dark mode, and as of this baseline six component spots still hardcode it (see `design-review/00-baseline.md`).
278: - **Don't** create long cyan or yellow background fields (banners, section washes) — they break the Online-Indicator Rule and the print-on-paper register.

  Line 124: Two themes, one material. Dark is the default state (deep navy console); light is the "paper mode" — but both use the same utility aliases, because `bg-white`, `border-black` and `text-black` are tokens (`--color-white`, `--color-black`) that flip per theme. New work must use the token vars, not literal hexes, or themes drift apart.

## User

Analyze all Git changes in my current Tojiwan Portfolio repository and generate an accurate, professional Git commit message.

**Context:**
I have completed a 15-step UI/UX improvement workflow using Impeccable and Playwright MCP, covering design analysis, layout, typography, color, responsiveness, animations, accessibility, performance, and final polish.

**Instructions:**

1. Run `git status` and inspect the actual changes using `git diff`, `git diff --staged`, and `git diff --stat`.
2. Include untracked files in the review, especially the `design-review/` documentation.
3. Read relevant design-review reports to understand the purpose of the changes.
4. Identify the most significant changes made to the project.
5. Group related changes logically.
6. Generate a meaningful Conventional Commit message.
7. Use a concise subject line, ideally under 72 characters.
8. Include a descriptive commit body summarizing the major improvements.
9. Do not claim changes were made unless supported by the actual Git diff or new files.
10. Do not stage, commit, or push anything automatically.

**Commit format:**

```text
<type>(<scope>): <short description>

- Summary of major UI improvements
- Summary of responsive and accessibility changes
- Summary of functionality and performance improvements
- Summary of documentation updates
```

Choose the most appropriate type (`feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `style`, `perf`, or `docs`) based on the actual changes.

If multiple independent commits would be better, recommend how to split them and provide separate commit messages.

**Output:**
- Recommended Git commit message
- Brief explanation of why it accurately represents the changes
- Optional alternative shorter commit message

Generate the message only. Wait for my approval before performing any Git operations that change repository state.

### What matters most

- **1.4s first paint:** content appears quickly.
- **80ms blocking time:** JavaScript isn’t heavily blocking interaction.
- **0 layout shift:** excellent—content stays in place while loading.
- **2.9s largest paint:** the main improvement opportunity; aim for **≤2.5s**.
- **4.4s Speed Index:** the page takes a little longer to look visually complete.

### My recommendation

**Keep this version and optimize selectively.** Prioritize investigating the LCP element and its loading/render delay, then the **81 KiB of estimated unused JavaScript**. The **150ms render-blocking** opportunity is smaller. These estimates aren’t guaranteed savings.

I wouldn’t sacrifice the portfolio’s personality just to chase 100. **92 with stable layout and low blocking time is a good launch result.**

One correction to our earlier assessment: localhost LCP measurements weren’t meaningful for visitor performance; this throttled production report is much more useful.

*Limits: this is one lab run; there’s insufficient real-user data yet. Accessibility 100 means automated checks passed, not that every accessibility scenario is covered.*

1: # Tojiwan Portfolio
2: 
3: Jake Andrei R. Peralta's portfolio for web development, Shopify, and automation work. Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Motion.
4: 
5: Light-default "paper mode" styling with a persistent dark console toggle, terminal-inspired panels, and a cyan robot-terminal logo. The site uses only self-hosted Courier Prime and IBM Plex Mono, with Courier Prime for headings, including the hero.
6: 
7: ## Development
8: 
9: ```bash
10: npm ci
11: npm run dev
12: ```
13: 
14: Open [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).
15: 
16: ## Checks and production
17: 
18: ```bash
19: npm run lint
20: npm run build
21: npm start
22: ```
23: 
24: ## Content
25: 
26: - `src/data/projects.ts`: project summaries, stacks, and optional `liveUrl`, `demoUrl`, `demoPassword`, and `designUrl` fields. Links render only when provided. Shop.Co includes a Shopify demo, a revealable demo password, and Figma design credit. Demo passwords are public visitor-access information, not private credentials.
27: - `src/data/skills.ts`: skills, services, and experience in newest-first order.
28: - `src/components/sections/tech-stack-section.tsx`: keyboard-accessible toolbox tabs and skill-to-SVG mappings. Logo assets live in `public/Icons/`; update the mapping when adding a skill.
29: - `src/components/sections/`: hero, About, projects, and contact content.
30: - `public/files/`: the downloadable CV linked from the hero and footer.
31: - `src/components/layout/site-footer.tsx`: Resources links and the ASCII Tojiwan wordmark.
32: - `src/app/icon.svg`: robot-terminal logo shared by the navbar and SVG favicon. Keep `src/app/favicon.ico` in sync when changing the mark.
33: 
34: External website links open in a new tab. Section links navigate within the page; email and phone links use the visitor's associated app.
35: 
36: ## Site URL
37: 
38: Set `SITE_URL` to the full deployed origin, including `https://`, in your hosting environment before building. Social image URLs use this value. If omitted, the site uses `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL` on Vercel or `http://localhost:3000` locally. Rebuild after changing it.
39: 
40: ## Features and integrations
41: 
42: - The contact form sends through Formspree with validation, sending/success/error feedback, and a spam honeypot. Direct email and profile links are also available. The owner confirmed a successful localhost submission and inbox delivery from the 2026-10-16 test.
43: - Hero portraits use all five `public/Profile_Avatar/pfp-*_result.webp` images in original color, starting with pfp-1. Mouse entry or click/tap/keyboard activation advances the image and wraps after pfp-5; a mouse click within 350ms of hover is ignored to avoid a double advance. <skill_content name="impeccable">
# Skill: impeccable

This skill gives you the tools and permission to create design that earns to be called out-of-distribution craft: Whereas before, your design work would have been safe, timid and measured, you now approach every design task as an award-winning design director with impeccable understanding for what makes exceptional design work: production-grade code, peak creativity, a clear POV, deep understanding of the needs of the client and users, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Go all out. No hedging, no shortcuts. The deliverable must be complete (except assets the user must provide).
- Dream big and bold. Distinct, beautiful, outstanding and highly inspiring work.
- Verify in bounded passes, not a loop, and the ceiling covers the whole cycle: screenshots, defect scans, micro-edits, and rebuilds alike. Build fully, inspect once with a batched round (desktop and mobile together on the web; the shipped device classes on a native platform), fix everything it shows in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, and stop polishing. Open-ended self-QA burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.opencode/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

## Commands

| Command | Category | Description | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `craft [feature]` | Build | Deprecated alias for an ordinary new-work request | [reference/craft.md](reference/craft.md) |
| `shape [feature]` | Build | Plan UX/UI before writing code | [reference/shape.md](reference/shape.md) |
| `init` | Build | Capture durable product context in PRODUCT.md | [reference/init.md](reference/init.md) |
| `document` | Build | Generate DESIGN.md from existing project code | [reference/document.md](reference/document.md) |
| `extract [target]` | Build | Pull reusable tokens and components into design system | [reference/extract.md](reference/extract.md) |
| `critique [target]` | Evaluate | UX design review with heuristic scoring | [reference/critique.md](reference/critique.md) |
| `audit [target]` | Evaluate | Technical quality checks (a11y, perf, responsive) | [reference/audit.md](reference/audit.md) · native: [reference/audit.native.md](reference/audit.native.md) |
| `polish [target]` | Refine | Final quality pass before shipping | [reference/polish.md](reference/polish.md) |
| `bolder [target]` | Refine | Amplify safe or bland designs | [reference/bolder.md](reference/bolder.md) |
| `quieter [target]` | Refine | Tone down aggressive or overstimulating designs | [reference/quieter.md](reference/quieter.md) |
| `distill [target]` | Refine | Strip to essence, remove complexity | [reference/distill.md](reference/distill.md) |
| `harden [target]` | Refine | Production-ready: errors, i18n, edge cases | [reference/harden.md](reference/harden.md) |
| `onboard [target]` | Refine | Design first-run flows, empty states, activation | [reference/onboard.md](reference/onboard.md) |
| `animate [target]` | Enhance | Add purposeful animations and motion | [reference/animate.md](reference/animate.md) |
| `colorize [target]` | Enhance | Add strategic color to monochromatic UIs | [reference/colorize.md](reference/colorize.md) |
| `typeset [target]` | Enhance | Improve typography hierarchy and fonts | [reference/typeset.md](reference/typeset.md) |
| `layout [target]` | Enhance | Fix spacing, rhythm, and visual hierarchy | [reference/layout.md](reference/layout.md) |
| `delight [target]` | Enhance | Add personality and memorable touches | [reference/delight.md](reference/delight.md) |
| `overdrive [target]` | Enhance | Push past conventional limits | [reference/overdrive.md](reference/overdrive.md) |
| `clarify [target]` | Fix | Improve UX copy, labels, and error messages | [reference/clarify.md](reference/clarify.md) |
| `adapt [target]` | Fix | Adapt for different devices and screen sizes | [reference/adapt.md](reference/adapt.md) · native: [reference/adapt.native.md](reference/adapt.native.md) |
| `optimize [target]` | Fix | Diagnose and fix UI performance | [reference/optimize.md](reference/optimize.md) |
| `live` | Iterate | Visual variant mode: pick elements in the browser, iterate on alternatives | [reference/live.md](reference/live.md) |
| `generate [n] [action] [element]` | Iterate | Variants, versions, or alternatives of a named element to choose from in the live browser; no manual picking | [reference/generate.md](reference/generate.md) |

# PRODUCT.md

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Users

- Recruiters (primary): evaluating Jake for full-time and freelance web/Shopify/automation work; need to judge skill quickly from real evidence and reach him directly.
- Potential clients: small businesses needing websites, Shopify storefront customization, or workflow/chatbot automation (n8n).
- Fellow developers and collaborators: browsing code (GitHub link) and project approaches.

## Product Purpose

A single-page portfolio that showcases Jake Andrei R. Peralta's responsive websites, Shopify storefronts, and AI/workflow automation projects. Success: a recruiter or client understands his three specializations, sees concrete project evidence, and contacts him or downloads his CV.

## Positioning

One developer covering all three of web development, Shopify development, and automation — presented as equals, not a headline specialism plus sidelines. Real, inspectable work backs the claim (a live Shopify demo, n8n RAG chatbots, client and capstone projects) instead of adjectives. The "Tojiwan" developer persona gives it a distinct, memorable identity.

## Operating Context

- Recruiter evaluation happens fast on a single scrolling page: specialization clarity, project evidence, CV download, and contact paths must be reachable quickly.
- The three specialization pillars: web development, Shopify development, and automation. Two visitors matter most for contact: recruiters (full-time or freelance) and clients with a concrete project in mind.
- Jake operates from Pampanga, Philippines (UTC+8, Philippine Time). Native languages: Tagalog, Kapampangan, English.
- Deployment: Vercel. `SITE_URL` is unset in the repo; the production URL must be set per the README before social/canonical metadata resolves to the live origin.
- The contact form sends through Formspree (spam honeypot included). Formspree plan usage limits remain unverified.
- Demo passwords (e.g. Shop.Co's) are public visitor-access information, not private credentials.
- CV is a downloadable PDF asset in `public/files/`; the GitHub profile doubles as the code-evidence surface.

## Capabilities and Constraints

Confirmed functionality:

- Single page (Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Motion): hero, about, projects, tech stack/skills, experience, services, contact, footer.
- Persistent light/dark theme (light "paper mode" served by default; dark console on toggle) with a theme toggle.
- Reduced-motion support, keyboard accessibility commitments, and a skip-to-content link (README defines the pre-deployment browser checklist).
- Contact form via Formspree with sending/success/error states; locally verified delivery on 2026-10-16.
- Downloadable CV linked from hero and footer.

Constraints and explicitly undecided facts:

- No project screenshots or accessible galleries yet — deferred by the owner.
- Vehiserive details are owner-managed and deferred (spelling of the name also unconfirmed).
- Live URLs beyond the Shop.Co demo are unverified; add only verified links.
- Production `SITE_URL` value is not yet recorded.
- Vercel Speed Insights is mounted but data collection has not been verified in production.
- `src/data/*.ts` is the single content source for projects and skills/experience (newest-first order).

## Brand Commitments

Binding by owner decision (preserved verbatim, not expanded):

- The "Tojiwan" developer persona/wordmark, including the ASCII wordmark in the footer.
- The cyan robot-terminal logo (`src/app/icon.svg`), kept in sync with `favicon.ico`.
- CLI/terminal-inspired voice and labels.
- Neo-brutalist terminal aesthetic with square geometry, 2px borders, hard offset shadows, light-default "paper mode" themes with a persistent dark console (owner decision, 2026-10-20), graph-paper backgrounds, cyan #0ea5e9 accent, Courier Prime and IBM Plex Mono (self-hosted).
- "Preserve current branding — no redesign" is a standing instruction for all future work acting on this record.

## Evidence on Hand

- Six real projects in `src/data/projects.ts`: Shop.Co (live Shopify demo + public demo password + Figma design credit), Facebook RAG Chatbot and One Pampanga RAG Chatbot (company project, on hold), Telegram Budget Tracker, Ramen Makimura Website (internship contribution), Vehiserive (DHVSU capstone).
- Real experience records in `src/data/skills.ts`: Freelance Shopify Developer (Jan–Apr 2026); Tigernethost OPC (Web Developer & AI Automation Specialist, Jun–Dec 2025); Tigernethost OPC internship (Feb–May 2025).
- CV PDF: `public/files/Peralta, Jake Andrei R. (RESUME).pdf`.
- Five real portraits: `public/Profile_Avatar/pfp-*_result.webp`.
- Self-hosted fonts with OFL licenses in `public/fonts/`.
- Education: BS Information Technology, Don Honorio Ventura State University (2021–2025).
- Absences that future work must not fabricate: no testimonials, no performance benchmarks, no verified client list, no deployment analytics yet.

## Product Principles

1. Evidence beats claims: every specialization is proven by real, inspectable work — demos, code, and case facts, never invented proof.
2. Trio as equals: web development, Shopify development, and automation always appear with equal weight; no single pillar outranks the others in positioning.
3. Recruiter-first legibility: specializations, project evidence, CV, and contact paths are reachable with minimal scrolling or hunting.
4. Honest status labels: on-hold, deferred, and unanswered items stay labeled as such.
5. Persona supports, never obscures: the Tojiwan terminal persona adds character but clarity and usability always win over novelty.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

- Keyboard operability for all interactive widgets (tabs with arrow keys, mobile menu Escape-close, password reveal, portrait cycler) is a product standard, not an afterthought.
- Visible focus states in both themes.
- `prefers-reduced-motion` switches animations off gracefully.
- Text and border contrast must hold across persistent dark and light themes.
- External links open in new tabs; in-page links navigate in place; email/phone links open the visitor's own apps.
